_sources: London Bat Group, Echolocation and bat detectors (https://londonbats.org.uk/bat-cave/echolocation-and-bat-detectos/); Maryland Department of Natural Resources, Bat Echolocation (https://dnr.maryland.gov/wildlife/pages/plants_wildlife/bats/batelocu.aspx). Accessed 2026-11-27.

dial.hear: A slow, loud 'chip... chop... chip... chop', high above the lamp.
dial.name: a noctule, flying high over the headland

dial.hear: Regular, dry clicks, low over the rain pool by the steps.
dial.name: a Daubenton's bat, skimming the pool

dial.hear: Irregular wet 'smacks', round and round the lamp.
dial.name: a common pipistrelle, circling the lamp

dial.hear: The same kind of smacks, but now at a higher setting. A second kind of bat shares the lamp.
dial.name: a soprano pipistrelle, circling the lamp

dial.hear: Nothing. Whatever is out here tonight is not calling at this setting.

buzz: Then, at 45, the smacks speed up and run together into a long buzz, like someone blowing a raspberry. Then nothing. Ruan says quietly: 'That was a moth.'

views.text: We know what it does: it calls, and it hears the echoes. That is all we can say.
views.reply: Neri, from the doorway: 'And that is a lot. We know the setting, the place, the catch. Science does not need to feel like the bat to know about the bat.'

views.text: Something like seeing with sound. But that is my picture, not the bat's.
views.reply: Ruan nods. 'Seeing with sound is a human sentence. It helps. It is also exactly the thing the bat does not have: words, and eyes to borrow them from.'

views.text: We cannot know at all. Even the detector turns its calls into our sounds.
views.reply: Ruan taps the detector. 'True: this box makes its call into something for my ears. But I still knew a moth was caught. Not knowing everything is not the same as knowing nothing.'
